findings.title: [P1] Restore socket listener removal during cleanup
findings.body: Calling the disposer returned by `attach` no longer removes the `"message"` listener. Messages continue reaching supposedly disposed handlers, while repeated attach/dispose cycles accumulate listeners, duplicate processing, and retained state.

findings.title: [P1] Restore polling interval cancellation during cleanup
findings.body: Calling the disposer returned by `startPolling` no longer clears its interval. Polling therefore continues after teardown, repeated lifecycle starts accumulate timers, and an active timer can prevent Node.js processes or tests from exiting.

findings.title: [P2] Restore removal of the socket message handler
findings.body:
After callers invoke the returned cleanup while the socket remains active, subsequent `"message"` events still invoke the stale handler. Reattachment also accumulates duplicate listeners and retained state.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P2] Restore cancellation of the polling interval
findings.body:
After callers invoke the returned stop function, `refresh` continues running every second indefinitely. This causes work and state updates after teardown and can keep a Node.js process alive.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Restore listener removal in the returned cleanup
findings.body:
Calling the cleanup returned by `attach` no longer unregisters the handler. Any subsequent `"message"` still invokes code expected to be disposed, and repeated attach/cleanup cycles accumulate listeners and memory.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Preserve and clear the polling interval during cleanup
findings.body:
The returned cleanup no longer stops the interval. After cleanup, `refresh` continues running every second indefinitely; in Node environments the active timer can also prevent process or test shutdown.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P2] Restore message-listener removal during teardown
findings.body:
On a long-lived socket receiving peer-controlled messages, invoking the returned disposer no longer revokes the handler. A peer can therefore trigger stale authorization/session logic after teardown; repeated attach/dispose cycles also retain handlers and amplify CPU and memory use per message.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P2] Cancel polling intervals when disposed
findings.body:
Every polling job now survives teardown indefinitely, retaining its callback and continuing privileged or expensive work. In a service where an attacker can repeatedly trigger poller creation, this permits unbounded timer accumulation and eventual availability loss.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Restore interval cancellation in the cleanup callback
findings.body:
After `startPolling` is called, invoking its returned cleanup function leaves the interval active forever. Each lifecycle restart accumulates another timer and callback, and in Node.js the referenced interval can prevent process shutdown.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Restore listener removal in the cleanup callback
findings.body:
Calling the disposer returned by `attach` no longer removes the `"message"` listener. Repeated attach/cleanup cycles retain handlers and their captured state, cause duplicate processing, and can eventually trigger listener-limit warnings or unbounded memory growth.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._
